newsitem.title: USA: AT&T to increase business market investment.
newsitem.headline: AT&T to increase business market investment.

text.p: AT&T Corp said on Monday that it would dramatically increase investment in its business markets area in 1997 to $5 billion from $3 billion in 1996, to meet the strong revenue growth offered by the data marketplace.
"We will grow both revenue and earnings at double-digit rates over this period (in business markets)," said Jeff Weitzen, executive vice president for At&T business markets.

AT&T said the entire marketplace they were addressing was growing at between 11 percent and 14 percent per year and At&T would exceed that in the fast-growing data services such as asynchronous transfer mode (ATM) and frame relay.
"Over the next three to four years data traffic will surpass voice traffic on the network," AT&T Chairman Robert Allen said.
AT&T's total capital expenditure in 1997 is expected to be $8-9 billion, compared with $6 billion in 1996, the company said.
Weitzen said in wireless and Internet services AT&T would grow at about the market rate and at somewhat less than the market rate for private lines.
Of the capital spending, about two thirds would go on the various data services, Weitzen said, though he pointed out that this would help support the growth of Internet services too.

Weitzen said that AT&T had increased its market share in frame relay by 5 percentage points in 1996, and had grown rapidly in web site hosting. AT&T began web hosting in the fourth quarter of 1996 and now hosts 3,000 sites.
"We've got great momentum going into 1997," he said.

AT&T said that it expected UniSource, its international telecommunications alliance, to grow dramatically in 1997, and noted this would be achieved on lower capital spending than its two main rivals, Concert Plc and Global One.
Concert is owned by merger partners British Telecommunications Plc and MCI Communications Corp. Global One is owned by Sprint Corp, France Telecom and Deutsche Telekom AG.
Analysts have criticized AT&T for what they saw as a low-key approach to the fast-growing international marketplace, and for the loose nature of the alliance. But Weitzen rejected this.
"Quite frankly, I'm getting tired of the loose alliance criticism," Weitzen said.

Weitzen said that AT&T had made great progress in quality control to eliminate fraud which had contributed to a rise in bad debt in the fourth quarter of 1997. However, he acknowledged that uncollectable revenues were likely to remain higher than hitherto because of the changed nature of the telecom marketplace, in which businesses are able to switch suppliers even when they have not paid all their bills.
